673.title: Read to the sick
673.hook: ten perceptions read to the sick monk Girimananda, who recovers
673.howItsDone: In parts of the Theravada world, monks chant the Girimananda Sutta for the sick, and visiting and reading to ill people, lay or ordained, is a long-standing Buddhist act of care.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the eleven blessings of metta, and your line, wish one person well. How was the night? Today, a new week, and a different bedside: someone who is ill. Day six hundred seventy-three.

When someone we love is sick, we bring things. Soup, flowers, a phone charger, a magazine nobody reads. What we really want to bring is something that helps, and we often don't know what that is. In the Book of Tens, a monk named Girimananda is sick, in pain, gravely ill. Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, comes to the Buddha and asks him to visit, out of compassion. The Buddha does something unexpected. He doesn't go himself. He sends Ananda back with something to bring. Not medicine. A list of ten things to read aloud. Today: sanna.
screen: `WHAT DO WE BRING THE SICK?` → `GIRIMANANDA IS GRAVELY ILL.` → `ANANDA IS SENT WITH A LIST.`

segments.voice: If you go to Girimananda, the Buddha says, and tell him the ten perceptions, it's possible his illness will subside at once. Then he gives them. One, impermanence: the body, feelings, all of it, changing. Two, not-self: none of it is me or mine. Three, the unattractive: the body seen plainly, hair, skin, bones, the inside as well as the outside. Four, drawbacks: the body as a home for many illnesses, and the text names a long list of them, eye disease to fever. Five, abandoning: letting go of harmful thoughts. Six, dispassion. Seven, cessation. Eight, not delighting in the whole world. Nine, the impermanence of all that's made. And ten, mindfulness of breathing, given in full: breathing in long, breathing out long, and on through sixteen steps. Ananda learns them, goes to Girimananda, and recites them. And the text says Girimananda recovered from that illness. Notice what kind of list this is. It isn't comforting in the usual way. It doesn't say you'll be fine. It looks straight at the body, its fragility and its changes, and ends with the simplest thing a sick person can still do: breathe, and know they're breathing. One modern reading is that a mind steadied and less gripped by fear helps the body. The text itself doesn't explain it. It just says he recovered. In some Theravada communities, this sutta is still chanted for people who are ill.
screen: `THE BUDDHA SENDS ANANDA.` · `IMPERMANENCE, NOT-SELF.` · `ENDING WITH THE BREATH.` · then, large: `HE RECOVERED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read something kind to someone ill. Sit, and settle with the tenth perception, the breath. Breathing in long, know it. Breathing out long, know it. Now bring to mind someone who is unwell, near or far. Picture sitting beside them. What could you read or say that would steady them? A favorite line, a message, a memory. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer. Choose one thing, and plan to send it today. The bell holds the time.

sanna. The Pali word for perception, as in the ten perceptions Ananda carries to Girimananda's bedside in the Book of Tens, from impermanence to mindfulness of breathing, after which the monk recovers. Today's word.
Your line: ten perceptions. Today, send one steadying word to someone who's unwell, and take one long, known breath for them. Day six hundred seventy-three.

tell Ananda the monk must bear it.
fork.reveal: he teaches Ananda the ten perceptions to carry to the bedside. Ananda recites them, and Girimananda recovers.

what it means: the Buddha sent a sick monk ten clear-eyed perceptions, ending with the breath.
what a scholar hears: the fourth perception names dozens of diseases one by one, from eye disease to fever; the tenth gives the same sixteen breathing steps as MN 118.

674.title: Inspired, then calm
674.hook: when the mind is scattered, turn to an inspiring theme, then return
674.howItsDone: Some meditation teachers suggest recollecting the Buddha, a teacher or one's own good deeds when practice turns dull or restless, before returning to the main object such as the breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Girimananda's bedside, and your line, ten perceptions. Did you send a steadying word to someone unwell? Today, what to do when your own mind won't settle. Day six hundred seventy-four.

Ananda goes one morning to a dwelling of nuns. They sit with him and tell him how their practice is going, and it's going well. We dwell, they say, with our minds well established in the four foundations of mindfulness, and we notice a progress, one stage after another. Ananda is glad, and later he reports it to the Buddha. The Buddha agrees: so it is. And then he adds a frank note about how meditation goes. While someone is contemplating, he says, a fever can arise, or sluggishness, or the mind can scatter outward. What then? Today: inspired, then calm.
screen: `A VISIT TO THE NUNS.` → `IT'S GOING WELL.` → `BUT SOMETIMES...`

segments.voice: When you're contemplating the body, or feelings, or mind, or phenomena, the Buddha says, and a fever arises, or sluggishness, or the mind scatters outward, then direct the mind toward some inspiring sign. Something that lifts the heart. The Pali word, pasadaniya, means something that brings serene confidence. The sutta doesn't say what it is; it might be the Buddha, a teacher, a good deed you remember, a line you love. And then watch the sequence the text describes. When the mind is turned to the inspiring sign, gladness arises. From gladness, joy. With a joyful mind, the body grows calm. With a calm body, one feels happiness. A happy mind becomes concentrated. Then comes the second half, the part that's easy to skip. Having been lifted, you withdraw: you set the inspiring image down and return to the original practice. The text says the person then knows: I'm not thinking and examining; I'm mindful within, and at ease. Notice the order. Not grit your teeth and force it. Not give up and scroll. Lift the heart first, then come back. The Buddha calls this directed development. And he says there's also undirected development, for when the mind is already steady and doesn't need the detour. It's an honest teaching. The nuns' report was good news, and the Buddha's answer still makes room for scattered days, with a way back that starts with gladness.
screen: `THE MIND SCATTERS.` · `TURN TO AN INSPIRING SIGN.` · `GLADNESS, JOY, CALM.` · then, large: `THEN RETURN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring one inspiring image. Sit, and start with the breath. If the mind is busy or dull, don't fight it. Bring to mind one image that lifts you: a face you admire, a kind act you once saw, a sunrise, the Buddha's still figure, a line you love. Stay with it until a little gladness rises. Feel the body soften. Then, gently, set the image down, and come back to the breath, now with a lighter heart. The bell holds the time.
Inspired. When the mind scatters, the Buddha tells Ananda, turn it to an inspiring sign, let gladness and calm arise, then return to the practice. Today's word.
Your line: look for what lifts you. Today, when your mind frays, look for one thing that lifts you, let it work for a breath or two, then go back to the task. Day six hundred seventy-four.

screen: `DAY 674 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SIX WAYS TO BE DEAR.`

675.title: Six ways to be dear
675.hook: kindness in deed, word and thought, sharing, virtue and view held together
675.howItsDone: Buddhist monastic communities often teach the six saraniya dhammas as the basis of harmony in the sangha, and lay Buddhist groups sometimes take them as guidelines for family and community life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the nuns, the scattered mind, and your line, look for what lifts you. What lifted you? Today, from one mind to a whole community, and what keeps people close. Day six hundred seventy-five.

Every group that lasts, a family, a team, a congregation, a group chat that's somehow survived ten years, has some unspoken reasons it holds together. And every group that falls apart has reasons too. The early monastic community knew both. Monks quarreled; the texts don't hide it. At Kosambi, one sutta says, the monks were stabbing each other with words, and the Buddha taught them this same list. In the Book of Sixes, the Buddha names six qualities that, in his words, are worth remembering, because they create love and respect and lead to harmony, to unity, to not quarreling. The Pali name is saraniya: things to be remembered, or things that make you dear. Today: saraniya.
screen: `WHY GROUPS HOLD TOGETHER.` → `MONKS QUARRELED TOO.` → `SIX THINGS TO REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: The first three are about kindness, in three directions. One: acts of body done with loving-kindness toward your companions, both in public and in private. Two: words spoken with loving-kindness, both in public and in private. Three: thoughts held with loving-kindness, both in public and in private. That little phrase, in public and in private, is the heart of it. Anyone can be kind when watched. What builds trust is the kindness nobody sees. Four: sharing. Whatever you receive, even the contents of your alms bowl, you share it with those who keep the same practice, without holding back. For a monk who eats only what he's given, that's his meal. Five: virtue held in common. You keep the same precepts as your companions, unbroken, the kind the wise praise. Six: view held in common. You share the understanding that leads out of suffering. Notice how practical the order is. It starts with what everyone can do immediately, a kind act, a kind word, and moves toward what grows slowly, a shared way of seeing. And notice that none of the six is about getting others to like you. They're all things you give. Being dear, in this sutta, isn't something you chase. It's what grows around someone who acts, speaks and thinks with kindness, shares, and keeps faith with a common path.
screen: `KIND IN DEED, WORD, THOUGHT.` · `IN PUBLIC AND IN PRIVATE.` · `SHARE EVEN YOUR BOWL.` · then, large: `VIRTUE AND VIEW IN COMMON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share one thing. Sit, and settle. Bring to mind a group you belong to: a family, a workplace, a team, a circle of friends. Picture the faces. Now think of one thing you have that you could share with them today. Some food. Some time. A tool, a skill, a piece of good news, credit for a job well done. Picture offering it, freely, without keeping score. Then, for a breath or two, wish them all well, quietly, in private. The bell holds the time.

saraniya. The Pali word for qualities to be remembered or cordial, the six things in the Book of Sixes that create love and harmony: kindness in body, speech and mind, sharing, virtue and view in common. Today's word.
Your line: one unseen kindness. Today, do one kind thing for someone in your group that nobody will see. Day six hundred seventy-five.

options: keep it; you need your strength.
fork.reveal: the fourth way to be dear is sharing whatever you receive, even the contents of your bowl, freely with your companions.

original.note: Pali saraniya: to be remembered, cordial; the saraniya dhamma are qualities that make people dear to each other.

trapdoor: what you thought: a community holds together through rules.
what it means: AN 6.12 names six things that make people dear: kindness, sharing, virtue and view in common.
what a scholar hears: the same six appear in the Digha Nikaya's account of the Buddha's last days, among the conditions for the community's welfare.

676.title: Even his back ached
676.hook: the old Buddha warms his back in the sun; Ananda sees his skin loosen
676.tomorrow: A friend gives the hard thing
676.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often tell this scene when teaching on aging and impermanence, and in Buddhist communities caring for elders, including elderly monks and nuns, is counted as a meritorious act.

segments.voice: Yesterday: saraniya, kindness in public and in private, and the shared bowl. Did you do one unseen kindness? Today, a quiet scene between an old teacher and his attendant. Day six hundred seventy-six.

Evening in Savatthi, at the Eastern Park, in the mansion of Migara's mother. The Buddha has come out of his afternoon seclusion. He's an old man now. He sits in the western sun, warming his back. Ananda, his attendant, comes over and begins to rub his limbs with his hands. It's the kind of moment people who care for an aging parent describe: hands on their arms, and suddenly the skin seems thinner than you remembered. Ananda notices. And he says it out loud. Today: jara.
screen: `AN OLD MAN IN THE SUN.` → `ANANDA RUBS HIS LIMBS.` → `HE NOTICES.`

segments.voice: It's wonderful, sir, Ananda says, it's amazing. Your complexion is no longer clear and bright. Your limbs are slack and wrinkled. Your body is bent forward. And there's a change in your senses: the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body. It's a blunt thing to say to your teacher. The Buddha doesn't flinch. So it is, Ananda, he says. In youth one is subject to aging; in health, to sickness; in life, to death. The complexion is no longer clear, the limbs are slack, the body is bent, the senses change. Then he speaks a verse that turns on aging itself, scolding it: shame on you, wretched old age, maker of ugliness. Even someone who lives a hundred years, he says, is bound for death; aging spares no one, it crushes everything. And then, the text says, he gets up, and goes into town for alms. That last detail is the whole teaching. He names it, he scolds it in verse, and then he goes on with the day. Elsewhere in the canon there are other glimpses: a day when his back hurts and he asks Sariputta to teach in his place while he lies down to rest it. The texts don't hide the Buddha's body. They show it aging, aching, ordinary. Some readers find that a comfort. Awakening, in this telling, didn't exempt even him from an old man's back. Even his.
screen: `YOUR SKIN IS LOOSE, SIR.` · `SO IT IS, ANANDA.` · `A VERSE AGAINST OLD AGE.` · then, large: `THEN HE GOES FOR ALMS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for an aging body. It might be your own, or someone else's. Sit, and turn your back toward a window or a warm lamp if you can. Let your hands rest on your forearms, and feel the skin, the warmth, the years in it. Breathe. Then bring to mind someone older whom you love. Picture warming their back, rubbing their arms, without hurry. Notice what tenderness feels like. Then think of one real thing you could do for an aging body this week, yours or theirs. The bell holds the time.
jara. The Pali and Sanskrit word for old age, spoken by the aging Buddha to Ananda in the evening sun: so it is; even life in the body ends in this. Today's word.
Your line: even his. Today, when your body creaks or someone you love slows down, remember: even his, and then go on with the day, gently. Day six hundred seventy-six.

screen: `DAY 676 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A FRIEND GIVES THE HARD THING.`

677.title: A friend gives the hard thing
677.hook: seven marks of a friend: gives what is hard to give, does what is hard to do, bears what is hard to bear
677.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers sometimes pair this sutta with the Buddha's teaching on good friendship, kalyanamittata, and lay Buddhists may read it as advice both for choosing friends and for being one.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the old Buddha in the sun, and your line, even his. Did your body or someone else's ask for care? Yesterday's scene was also a friendship: Ananda's hands on his teacher's arms. Today, what makes a friend. Day six hundred seventy-seven.

Three in the morning, and the phone rings. Who would you call back? Who would call you? Not the people who like your posts. The ones who'd pick up. That list is often short, and it doesn't always match the people we see the most. The Book of Sevens has a short sutta that tries to put that list into words. It's addressed to the monks, but nothing in it is monastic. It's seven marks of a friend worth keeping close. Today: mitta.
screen: `WHO WOULD PICK UP AT 3AM?` → `NOT ALWAYS WHO WE SEE MOST.` → `SEVEN MARKS OF A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: A friend with seven qualities, the Buddha says, is worth associating with. One: they give what is hard to give. Two: they do what is hard to do. Three: they bear what is hard to bear. Four: they tell you their secrets. Five: they keep your secrets. Six: they don't abandon you in misfortune. Seven: they don't look down on you when you're ruined. Notice the first three. Hard to give, hard to do, hard to bear. Anyone can give what's easy: a like, a quick text, the thing they didn't need anyway. A friend is the one who gives what costs something. Their Saturday. Their honesty, when it's awkward. The patience to sit through your bad month. Then four and five, a pair: trust going both ways. They let you in, and they don't let your life out. And six and seven: the friend who stays when things fall apart, and who doesn't treat you differently when you've lost. That last one is sharp: it's easy to stay close to someone doing well. The sutta ends in verse, repeating the seven, and closes by saying that whoever wants a friend should seek out a person like this. Two days ago, the six ways to be dear described what makes a community hold. This is the same thing at the size of two people. And the sutta can be read both ways at once: a list of friends to look for, and a list of how to be one.
screen: `HARD TO GIVE, DO, BEAR.` · `SECRETS SHARED, SECRETS KEPT.` · `STAYS IN MISFORTUNE.` · then, large: `A FRIEND GIVES THE HARD THING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be one of the seven. Sit, and settle. Bring to mind a friend who once gave you something hard: time, honesty, patience, presence when things were bad. Let yourself feel grateful for a few breaths. Then turn it around. Bring to mind a friend who might need something hard from you right now. Which of the seven could you be for them this week? Give the hard thing, bear the hard thing, keep the secret, stay. Choose one. The bell holds the time.

mitta. The Pali word for friend, root of metta, behind the seven marks in the Book of Sevens: a true friend gives, does and bears what's hard, shares secrets, and stays through misfortune and ruin. Today's word.
Your line: give something that costs you. Today, give one friend something that costs you a little: time, attention, an honest word. Day six hundred seventy-seven.

678.title: Pleasure without the hook
678.hook: the monk is taught to eat like a traveler eating to cross the desert
678.howItsDone: Theravada monks and nuns recite a daily reflection on the purpose of food before eating, and many lay Buddhists practice mindful eating, pausing before a meal to consider what it is for.

segments.voice: Yesterday: seven marks of a friend, and your line, give something that costs you. What did you give? Today, something we do three times a day, and one of the hardest images in the canon. Day six hundred seventy-eight.

A fair warning first: today's image is meant to be hard to hear. The early texts sometimes reach for a shocking picture on purpose, so that a point can't slide past. Eleven days ago, giving food was life itself. Today, the other side: eating, and the hook that can hide in it. The bag of chips that empties itself. The second dessert nobody wanted. In the Connected Sayings, in a chapter on what the texts call the four kinds of nutriment, the Buddha asks the monks how they should regard their daily food. And he answers with a parable about two travelers in a desert. Today: ahara.
screen: `A HARD IMAGE, ON PURPOSE.` → `THE HOOK IN EATING.` → `TWO TRAVELERS, A DESERT.`

segments.voice: A husband and wife set out across a desert with a little food, and with their only son, a child they love dearly. Halfway across, the food runs out. There is no other way to survive. In the parable, they do the unthinkable: weeping, they eat their own child's flesh, to reach the other side. The Buddha then asks: would they eat that food for fun? For pleasure, for decoration, for beauty? No, the monks answer. They'd eat it only to cross the desert. That, the Buddha says, is how to regard ordinary food. The image is deliberately unbearable. Nobody could enjoy that meal, and nobody would take one bite more than needed. That's the point: just enough to cross. Monks still say a daily reflection, found elsewhere in the canon, that carries the same sense in gentler words: I eat not for fun, not for intoxication, not for looks, but only to keep this body going, to end hunger, and to support the holy life. The teaching isn't that food is bad, or that taste is wrong. Lay Buddhists cook beautiful food and offer it with joy. The hook is the extra: eating to fill a mood, to escape, to keep chasing a pleasure that ended three bites ago. The parable asks a simple question at every meal. What is this for? If the answer is to cross, to live, to be well, the pleasure that comes with it has no hook in it.
screen: `FOOD RUNS OUT IN THE DESERT.` · `THEY EAT ONLY TO CROSS.` · `NOT FOR FUN, NOT FOR LOOKS.` · then, large: `JUST ENOUGH TO CROSS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat one meal simply. Sit now, and settle. Picture your next meal on the table in front of you. Before you eat it, ask the parable's question: what is this for? Let the honest answer come: hunger, energy, comfort, company. Then picture eating it slowly, tasting each bite, and noticing the moment when you've had enough. Not the moment the plate is empty. The moment you've crossed. The bell holds the time.

ahara. The Pali and Sanskrit word for nutriment or food, behind the parable of the desert travelers in the Connected Sayings: eat as they did, only to cross, and the meal has no hook in it. Today's word.
Your line: just enough to cross. Today, at one meal, stop at enough, and notice how the body feels an hour later. Day six hundred seventy-eight.

screen: `DAY 678 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE POT AND THE LID.`

679.title: The pot and the lid
679.hook: like a water pot turned upside down, nothing stays in; an upright pot fills
679.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers sometimes use the three pots when encouraging students to review and practice what they hear, and in some communities Dhamma talks are followed by recitation or discussion to help the teaching stay.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the desert travelers, and your line, just enough to cross. Did you stop at enough? Today closes a week, with a question about how we listen. Day six hundred seventy-nine.

Look back at this week. Girimananda's bedside. The nuns and the inspiring sign. Six ways to be dear. The old Buddha in the evening sun. Seven marks of a friend. The desert crossing. That's a lot of teaching in seven days. Now an honest question: how much of it stayed? The Book of Threes has a sutta for exactly that question. It sorts listeners into three kinds, using three homely pictures: a pot turned upside down, a lap full of snacks, and a pot standing the right way up. Today: avakujja.
screen: `A WEEK OF TEACHINGS.` → `HOW MUCH STAYED?` → `THREE KINDS OF LISTENER.`

segments.voice: The first listener goes often to hear the teaching. The teaching is good in the beginning, middle and end. But they don't attend to any of it, not while sitting, not after they get up. That person, the Buddha says, is like a pot turned upside down. Pour water on it, and it all runs off. The second listener follows while sitting. They get the beginning, the middle and the end. But once they stand up, it's gone. That one is like a person with sesame seeds and rice cakes in their lap, who forgets and stands up, and everything scatters on the ground. The third listener takes it in while sitting and still holds it after getting up. That one is like a pot standing upright. Pour water in, and it stays. So, about today's title: there is no lid in the sutta. There's an upside-down pot, a lap and an upright pot. The lid is our word, and it's a fair one. Plenty of us listen with a lid on: the phone in one hand, the reply already half-composed. Notice that the first two listeners aren't lazy. They show up. They sit through the whole thing. The difference is the angle of the pot. Turning it upright is something you can do: recall a teaching later, repeat it to someone, try it once. That's what the carry has been asking of you every day this week.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen with an upright pot. Sit, and settle. Picture a clay pot resting in your lap, mouth up. Now, one at a time, let this week's lines pour in: ten perceptions. Inspired, then calm. Six ways to be dear. Even his. A friend gives the hard thing. Just enough to cross. Which ones stayed in? Which ran off? No grading. Pick the one that matters most to you, and hold it for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
avakujja. The Pali word for upside down, naming the first of three listeners in the Book of Threes: an upside-down pot, a spilling lap, and an upright pot that holds what's poured in. Today's word.
Your line: keep the pot upright. Today, next time someone tells you something that matters, repeat it back once, later in the day. Day six hundred seventy-nine.
